analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Clean Air Act's acid rain program that limits power plant sulfur dioxide pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the Clean Air Act's acid rain controls, died in committee with zero cosponsors and never came to a vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted Title IV of the Clean Air Act — the section that controls acid rain by requiring power plants, especially coal-burning ones, to cut their sulfur dioxide emissions. Wiping out that section would have let those plants emit more pollution that falls as acid rain on lakes, forests, and buildings downwind. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been coal-fired electric utilities and producers of high-sulfur coal, which would have been freed from the sulfur dioxide reduction requirements that Title IV imposes. Plants in the Midwest and East that burn high-sulfur coal faced the largest cleanup costs under the acid rain program.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Title IV of the Clean Air Act, the acid deposition control title, in its entirety.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on people who breathe air downwind of coal plants and on ecosystems: acid rain from sulfur dioxide emissions damages lakes and streams, forests, crops, and buildings, and sulfur pollution contributes to fine-particle smog that harms human health.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Title IV would have undone the program that requires utilities to cut sulfur dioxide emissions, allowing more acid rain on lakes, forests, and communities downwind of coal plants.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that utilities had already begun investing in compliance with the acid rain program — buying low-sulfur coal and scrubbers — and repeal would have disrupted those investments while stripping away air quality protections people had counted on.
The bill had no cosponsors, signaling even other members who opposed regulation saw no path or appetite for full repeal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — sparing utilities and high-sulfur coal producers the cost of emission cuts — comes entirely at the expense of cleaner air for everyone downwind. It offered nothing in return to the public, which is one reason it drew no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the two-year Congress ended with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Tom DeLay introduced the bill on October 6, 1994, in the final weeks of the 103rd Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
No further action was taken, and the bill never received a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People downwind of coal-fired power plants came out ahead: the acid rain program stayed on the books, and utilities remained required to cut sulfur dioxide emissions. The bill never gained traction even within its own party's conference.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downwind residents; the acid rain rules survived

for.name: Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act's acid rain title.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee chair in the 103rd Congress; the bill was referred to his committee and never reported out or scheduled for a vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction over the Clean Air Act
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 6, 1994, and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced the repeal bill with no cosponsors of either party in a Democratic-controlled House, and the Democratic-led committee let it die without action.

industries.note: Repealing Title IV would have eliminated the sulfur dioxide reduction obligations that utilities burning high-sulfur coal face under the acid rain program. The industry's gain would have come directly as more pollution falling on the public downwind.
The acid rain program pushed power plants toward low-sulfur coal and scrubbers, reducing demand for high-sulfur coal; repeal would have restored demand for the dirtier product.
Title IV's emission limits created a large market shift toward low-sulfur coal; repeal would have erased part of that demand advantage.
